title: researchED Melbourne Returns
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Ashman recounts attending researchED Melbourne 2026 as a guest rather than a speaker or organizer for the first time in a decade of involvement with the conference series, offering an inside view of the day's keynotes and sessions. He highlights Haileybury principal and ACARA board chair Derek Scott's framing of the school as an early adopter of explicit teaching, Canadian mathematics education researcher Anna Stokke's keynote on research scepticism, and a panel discussion that surfaced the politically charged question of the NAPLAN gender gap in numeracy, which Ashman notes is only one of five gender gaps in the assessment. He describes sessions on cognitive science ('thinking hard'), England's multi-academy-trust model as a possible preview for Australian school reform, and a conversation about the risks of imposing a single 'Instructional Hierarchy' as a uniform lesson-plan structure across all subjects. Ashman is careful to flag his own reservations, noting that 'desirable difficulties' is at risk of being misused to justify unsupported 'productive struggle' strategies, and that subject teams -- not whole-school mandates -- should generally own decisions about specific teaching techniques. The piece closes on an optimistic note about the roughly 400 attendees' collective potential to improve Australian education.
points: Shadow education minister Brad Rowswell told the conference each underserved child costs the state '$33 billion' if literacy and numeracy instruction isn't fixed -- a figure Ashman suspects was a slip of the tongue but notes signals evidence-informed teaching has become a rare point of cross-party agreement.

On the NAPLAN gender gap in numeracy, panelist Jordana Hunter pointed out that Singaporean girls outperform Australian boys even though Singapore also has a gender gap -- complicating simple explanations for the Australian pattern.

Ashman flags a specific concern about the 'Instructional Hierarchy' being interpreted as a uniform, school-wide lesson-plan structure, arguing those decisions need to be made by subject teams, not imposed top-down.

He cites his own school's experience with mini-whiteboards as a model for good practice adoption: English teachers were allowed years of uncertainty before choosing, with the help of Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion videos, to take ownership of the technique themselves.
Matt Hood's panel on multi-school organisations, now being piloted in Tasmania, is framed by Ashman as Australia looking at reforms England enacted roughly fifteen years earlier.
quotes: As we all sat in a large space on the ninth floor, he reminded us that Haileybury was a pioneer of explicit teaching, first trialling it in 2007/8.
He referred to research suggesting that each child costs the state $33 billion if we don't get this right. That sounds like a lot and I suspect he misspoke.
Although a genuine matter of concern, I do find it interesting that this is one of five NAPLAN outcomes, with girls outperforming boys on the other four.
I worry a little that desirable difficulties, the concept at the core of Clark's talk, has been misused to argue for so-called productive struggle strategies.

I am nervous about applying uniform models of learning in a school, especially a universal lesson plan structure -- which is how it seemed the Instructional Hierarchy was being interpreted in this case.

I remember that for several years, the English teachers at my school were unsure whether mini whiteboards had anything to offer their subject. Eventually, with the help of resources such as Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion videos, they began to experiment and took ownership of mini whiteboards for themselves.
